clue.text: Pure and simple start of crossword-quick !

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, taken here from crossword

parts.note: 'quick!' as a command means make haste, so haste

explanation.surface: A solver boasts of a plain, honest crossword that can be finished fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of' takes C from crossword; the exclamation 'quick!' is the urging 'haste!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste style is plain and unadorned, while a chaste person is morally pure, so both halves of the phrase fit.

clue.text: Vital decisions made here by rule of thumb

definitions.text: Vital decisions made here by rule of thumb

parts.words: Vital decisions made here by rule of thumb
parts.note: the arena of Rome where the crowd or emperor decided a gladiator's life or death with thumbs up or down

explanation.surface: A place where important choices are made by rough guesswork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital' means life-or-death, and 'rule of thumb' is taken literally: a thumb signal decided a defeated gladiator's fate.
explanation.definitionFit: The great amphitheatre of ancient Rome hosted gladiator combats where thumbs signalled life or death.

clue.text: A current stoppage — worker yielding, nothing

parts.note: a dam stops a river's current
a worker is an ant, in crossword convention

explanation.surface: An industrial dispute: a strike halts power while the labourer gives way.
explanation.walkthrough: A, DAM (it stops a current) and ANT (worker). The definition reads as 'yielding nothing', i.e. unyielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unshakeable in a decision gives no ground at all, yielding nothing.

clue.text: I knew match could be settled here

indicators.note: a match settled can be sorted out, so the letters are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone recalls where the outcome of a game was decided.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of I KNEW MATCH are rearranged. Twickenham, in south-west London, is the home ground of English rugby union, so a match could indeed be settled there.
explanation.definitionFit: The stadium in south-west London hosting England rugby union internationals is the place indicated by the word.

clue.text: Fighter cover deployed below clouds

explanation.surface: Warplanes give protection to troops beneath an overcast sky.
explanation.walkthrough: An air umbrella is the military term for a screen of fighter aircraft protecting ground forces; the second definition is the everyday rain shield opened under clouds.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighter cover is an air screen over troops in military jargon; the ordinary one is a rain shield opened when clouds threaten.

clue.text: Unlikely "capitalist"?

parts.note: a resident of the Soviet capital, a communist, so unlikely to be a capitalist, yet a dweller in a capital city

explanation.walkthrough: In the Cold War a Moscow citizen was the opposite of a capitalist, but an inhabitant of a capital is literally a capital-ist.
explanation.definitionFit: A Moscow native lives in a capital city, but under Soviet rule was hardly an advocate of free markets.

clue.text: May, to August clamour of oyster-fanciers ?

definitions.text: May, to August clamour of oyster-fanciers ?

parts.words: May, to August clamour of oyster-fanciers
parts.note: oysters are traditionally eaten only in months with an R, so from May to August the cry is that the letter R is gone; the word also means an uproar

explanation.surface: Seafood lovers grumble in summer when their favourite shellfish is unavailable.
explanation.walkthrough: May, June, July and August have no letter R, and tradition says oysters are only eaten in R months. Rout is an old word for a noisy disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic sense of the word is an uproar or noisy rabble, a clamour; split, it says R is absent.

clue.text: Spain and Portugal expel leader of this African state

parts.words: Spain and Portugal expel leader of this
parts.note: Iberia, the peninsula of Spain and Portugal, is what is left of the answer once its first letter is removed

explanation.surface: Two European countries banish the head of an African nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' is the answer: drop its leader and you get IBERIA, the peninsula holding Spain and Portugal.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberia is a republic on the West African coast, founded by freed American slaves.

clue.text: Al part of France not lacking, in skill

parts.note: the printed A1 (first-rate) supplies its letter A
a département, abbreviated dept, is an administrative part of France

explanation.surface: A first-rate French region is not short of talent.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints A1 (first-class), giving A; DEPT is short for département, the administrative division of France.
explanation.definitionFit: A skilled person is expert, someone who certainly does not lack ability.

clue.text: Fever in semi-detached house in Verona

indicators.note: half detached: half of the family name is cut away, leaving the other half

parts.note: the Montagues are Romeo's family, one of the two houses of Verona in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: Someone catches a fever while staying in a semi-detached house in an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'semi-detached' removes half of MONTAGUE, the first four letters MONT. A semi-detached house is one sharing a wall with its neighbour, common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a malarial fever with shivering fits.

clue.text: Starring in first act of play =

explanation.surface: An actor takes the main role in the opening act of a drama.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games the player who puts down the first card of a trick is said to lead, so the opening act of play is a lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A starring actor has the lead role; in cards, playing the first card of a round is the lead.

clue.text: First of September-fall, or nearly so

definitions.text: First of September-fall, or nearly so

indicators.note: the opening letter of the following word, September, is what is taken

parts.note: a tumble is a fall

explanation.surface: An autumn mishap: the start of September brings a tumble, or something close to one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of' gives S; fall is TUMBLE. The whole clue also describes the answer: a trip that is a fall, or nearly so.
explanation.definitionFit: To trip is to lurch and almost go down, which the whole clue describes as falling or nearly so.

clue.text: Plane for explorer

explanation.surface: An aircraft is named in honour of a famous polar adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Avro Shackleton was a British maritime patrol aircraft named after the Antarctic explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avro Shackleton was a postwar RAF patrol aircraft; Sir Ernest Shackleton led Antarctic expeditions.

clue.text: Worry shown by some highly-strung types

explanation.surface: Nervous, tense people show signs of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'highly-strung types' looks like nervous people but means stringed instruments, such as guitars, whose necks carry frets.
explanation.definitionFit: To be anxious is to fret; the raised ridges across a guitar neck are also frets.

clue.text: Awfully hot in odd periods of the holy office

indicators.note: in puts one rearranged group inside the other
odd means strange, so the letters of periods are rearranged
awfully suggests something badly done, so the letters of hot are mixed up

explanation.surface: A clergyman's role is unbearably warm at strange times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periods' are not times here but simply letters to shuffle, as 'odd' says; 'Awfully' works on 'hot' the same way, and 'in' sets the smaller group inside the larger.
explanation.definitionFit: The office of a priest, the ordained ministry of the clergy.

clue.text: Letter to nurses reveals how stretcher operates

parts.note: the letter X is spelt out as ex
to nurse someone is to tend them

explanation.surface: A note to hospital staff explains how patients on a stretcher are carried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' gives EX, the spelling of the letter X. The stretcher is not the medical one but anything that stretches, which lengthens.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that stretches lengthens or reaches further, which is exactly its operation.

clue.text: City of iron rising in quiet country area

indicators.note: in places the turned iron within the quiet country area

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
a field is an area of countryside

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A town known for its iron grows up amid peaceful farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' only works because this is a down clue, where reading upwards turns the iron symbol round. Sheffield in Yorkshire is famous for steel, so 'City of iron' is a fair surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheffield is a large Yorkshire city historically famous for steel and cutlery.

clue.text: Fashionable ways of aggression?

parts.note: something fashionable is in
roads are ways

explanation.surface: Trendy methods of attacking someone are discussed.
explanation.walkthrough: IN (fashionable) plus ROADS (ways); the whole clue also reads as a description of incursions into enemy territory.
explanation.definitionFit: Incursions or advances into hostile territory are routes of attack, hence ways of aggression.

clue.text: Alter sentences, if senior to Shakespeare's justice ?

indicators.note: alter means change, so the letters of sentences are changed in order

explanation.surface: A judge revises his rulings now that he has outranked a Shakespearean magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: In As You Like It's 'Seven Ages of Man', the justice is the fifth age; the ageing that follows it is older, so senior to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Growing old is the stage that follows the justice in the Seven Ages speech.

clue.text: Diameter's short-cut, arranged to connect opposite sides

indicators.note: arranged means the remaining letters are put in a new order
read as cut short: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a diameter is a line across a circle

explanation.surface: Geometry: a diameter is the quickest route linking the two sides of a circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short-cut' trims the R from DIAMETER, leaving DIAMETE, and 'arranged' shuffles those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between links two opposing parties to bring them to agreement.

clue.text: Diabolical writer

explanation.surface: An author is described as fiendish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The dickens' is an old euphemism for the devil, as in 'what the dickens'.
explanation.definitionFit: The dickens is a mild old oath meaning the devil; Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Philosopher makes point with a sort of sermon

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point

indicators.note: a sort of signals the following word reshaped into another arrangement

explanation.surface: A thinker makes his argument through something like preaching.
explanation.walkthrough: E (a compass point) followed by MERSON, the letters of SERMON rearranged as 'a sort of' suggests. Ralph Waldo Emerson was an American essayist and philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was the American transcendentalist thinker and essayist.

clue.text: A person of importance, but anonymous

explanation.surface: Someone important who nevertheless stays nameless.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable figure is called a somebody; used plainly the word means an unnamed individual.

clue.text: Prepare to shoot a bird

explanation.surface: A hunter readies his gun to fire at a game bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a gun's hammer readies it to fire; a male fowl is also so called.

clue.text: Raise one's standing in the country, say

indicators.note: say tells us to go by how the word is spoken

parts.note: a clime is a region or country, as in 'warmer climes'

explanation.surface: Someone wants to improve their status in the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: CLIME, an old word for a region or country, is pronounced like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to go up, so to rise socially is to go up the ladder.

clue.text: Frequently archaic and of "manifold" form?

parts.note: manifold means many times over, here taken as tenfold, or ten times

explanation.surface: Something old-fashioned recurs often and in many shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: OF taken as written, then 'manifold' read as multiplied many times: TEN TIMES. The answer is an old word for often.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for often, meaning many times.

clue.text: Off-stage direction

parts.note: the stage direction telling an actor to leave, and also a direction leading off the stage, a way out

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a stage direction sending an actor off, and as a route out.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin stage direction meaning 'he goes out' tells an actor to leave the stage; it is also a way out.

clue.text: 23 topped part of tree

indicators.note: topped means having its top cut off, and in a down clue the top is the first letter

parts.note: 23 refers to the answer at 23 down

explanation.surface: Someone tops a tree by sawing off a high bough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topped' removes the first letter of the answer to 23 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A large branch growing from a trunk is a bough.

clue.text: Though in quite miserable circumstances, don't be listless

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words quite miserable

explanation.surface: Even when you feel wretched, keep your energy up.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across quITE MISErable. 'listless' is read as without a list: to set things out item by item is to make one.
explanation.definitionFit: To set things out item by item is to draw up a list, the opposite of being without one.

clue.text: Elementary form of alcoholic's confession?

parts.note: a heavy drinker admitting the habit might say he drinks so much, using tope, an old verb for drinking to excess

explanation.surface: A drinker's admission is put in the simplest terms.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the second reading as I SO TOPE: tope is an old verb meaning to drink alcohol to excess. 'Elementary' refers to chemical elements.
explanation.definitionFit: A variant of a chemical element with a different neutron count is one form of that element.

clue.text: One who interferes with a working majority?

definitions.text: One who interferes with a working majority?

parts.words: One who interferes with a working majority?
parts.note: a meddler, punningly read as a group of people who are occupied, the busy main body

explanation.surface: Someone disrupts a government's comfortable parliamentary majority.
explanation.walkthrough: A working majority is a parliamentary term; read literally, a working majority is a busy main body.
explanation.definitionFit: A meddler is a person who pokes into other people's affairs.

clue.text: Most rum toddies leave one tiddly

indicators.note: tiddly, mildly drunk, signals the letters are jumbled

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Strange drinks: the last hot toddies leave someone slightly tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one I (one) out of TODDIES as 'leave' says, and shuffle the rest, TODDES, as 'tiddly' signals. 'Rum' here means strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is British slang for strange or peculiar, so the most rum is the strangest.
